title: Trajectory Matching: Discrete Flow Matching with Structured Actions
summary: Most discrete flow matching conditions only on endpoints and so is limited to independent, component-wise edits on fixed-size states. Trajectory matching instead conditions on a full sequence of user-defined actions connecting the endpoints (attach a fragment, add a node with its edge, grow a child), giving simulation-free training targets. They prove the objective recovers the marginal flow and strictly subsumes factorised DFM; on MOSES molecule generation validity rises from 92.8% to 99.2%.
takeaways: Conditioning on a whole action path rather than just endpoints makes non-factorising and size-changing actions tractable.
The marginal flow is still recovered, so this is a generalisation of DFM, not an approximation.
The action vocabulary becomes a modelling choice — domain-aligned actions help structured outputs.
relevance: Your lattice-simplex CTMC moves single counts between isoforms under a fixed gene total; this framework lets you define richer, structured moves (e.g. shifting mass between isoforms that share exons) while keeping a principled generator-matching target.

title: Generative Modeling via Nonlinear Schrödinger Bridges and Branching Diffusions
summary: The authors extend the Schrödinger bridge to a nonlinear version (SBNL) defined by coupled forward–backward PDEs from mean-field game theory, so the bridge can include interaction terms and convex penalties. They solve it with branching diffusions — a probabilistic representation of semilinear PDEs — which is embarrassingly parallel and scales to high dimension. The method recovers the classical bridge, handles Gross–Pitaevskii-type and potential interactions, and generates MNIST and FFHQ images; score-based diffusion and Gaussian Schrödinger bridges appear as special cases.
takeaways: Classical Schrödinger bridges are the linear case of a mean-field-game PDE system; adding nonlinearity lets samples interact.
Branching diffusions give a simulation-based, parallel solver for the resulting semilinear PDEs.
Diffusion models and tractable Gaussian bridges sit inside the framework as special cases.
relevance: Bridges between populations are a natural tool for perturbation modelling (control vs perturbed cells); the interaction term is a way to encode population-level constraints, such as matching a target marginal, which links to the Jeffrey guidance paper you read yesterday.

title: Closing the Modality Gap via Simplex-Constrained Representations
summary: Contrastive multimodal models like CLIP leave a persistent gap between image and text embeddings on the sphere. Moving the embeddings onto the probability simplex with lightweight softmax adapters and a Total Variation similarity reduces the centroid gap by 97–99% across five retrieval benchmarks while matching or beating retrieval of unconstrained models.
takeaways: Sphere and simplex share intrinsic dimension, but the simplex's non-negativity and unit-mass constraints act as a shared coordinate system.
TV distance replaces cosine similarity as the natural similarity on the simplex.
A purely geometric change, with small adapters, nearly closes the modality gap.
relevance: A spark: the simplex as a representation space rather than a data space. Your isoform proportions already live there — it's a nudge to think about which similarity (TV, Fisher–Rao, Aitchison) your models implicitly use on it.

title: Binary Discrete Diffusion: Candidate-Set Diffusion for Logic and Planning Tasks
authors: Casado Noguerales, von Rütte, Schölkopf, Hofmann & Raoufi
summary: Masked and uniform discrete diffusion destroy a token's identity in one jump, so noisy states can't express 'one of these few options'. Binary Discrete Diffusion is a continuous-time process whose state is a set of candidate tokens per position (a binary membership vector), changed by adding and removing candidates. It beats tuned masked and uniform baselines on Sudoku-Extreme, Boxoban and graph colouring, and stays competitive on language modelling.
takeaways: The choice of corruption kernel changes what the reverse model learns, not just its efficiency.
Candidate sets let information be lost and recovered gradually, representing partial uncertainty in the state itself.
Gains are largest on the hardest constraint-satisfaction instances.
relevance: A worked example of designing the forward CTMC kernel rather than defaulting to masking — directly relevant to your choice of noising process on the lattice simplex, where intermediate states could likewise encode partially resolved isoform assignments.

title: Internal Guidance as a Sampling Method for Tilted Diffusion Models
summary: Reward guidance samples an exponential tilt of the base density, usually via an extra drift term or reweighted transitions ('external guidance'). For discrete data on {−1,1}^d the authors show the denoiser of any linearly tilted density is exactly the base denoiser evaluated at a shifted, rescaled input, so guidance can change where the denoiser is evaluated instead. Training with random diagonal rescalings lets a single network handle these out-of-distribution inputs, sampling reward tilts, class labels and infilling without fine-tuning.
takeaways: Tilting can be implemented by moving the denoiser's input rather than adding a guidance term.
The exact result holds for linear tilts of discrete distributions embedded in the hypercube.
Training-time data augmentation (random rescalings) is what makes the shifted evaluations reliable.
relevance: Pairs naturally with today's Jeffrey guidance paper (also a tilt p(x)ρ(u(x))): together they give two routes — external vs internal — to steer a pretrained discrete generator like yours towards a target.

title: Compatible Likelihoods for Flow Matching on Manifolds
summary: On the flat 1D torus, the authors construct a case where a recent likelihood-based extension of Riemannian flow matching is optimised by a velocity field that pushes samples away from the data. They define 'compatibility' — the objective's population minimiser recovers the true marginal velocity — give a general condition for it, and propose an exponential-family objective over endpoints that is compatible and only puts mass on feasible velocities. It improves NLL on two of four sphere geospatial benchmarks and on high-dimensional tori.
takeaways: A flow matching loss can be globally optimal yet point the wrong way if it isn't compatible.
On compact manifolds, some objectives put density on infeasible velocities.
The fix amounts to a reweighting of the FM loss that treats speed and direction errors differently on constant-curvature manifolds.
relevance: A spark from geometry: the simplex in your work also has boundaries and feasibility constraints, and the 'is my loss's minimiser actually the marginal field?' check is a useful sanity test for any non-Euclidean flow matching variant you design.
Same design question as your source-conditioned models: what to put at t = 0. A gene-level prediction (as in scIso) could serve as the source, with the flow learning only the isoform-level residual.
summary: For combinatorial perturbations, most of the response is the sum of single-perturbation effects. SynGeneFlow anchors the flow's source distribution at that additive prior and learns only the residual flow to the true perturbed state.
takeaways: Choosing an informative source distribution focuses model capacity on the hard, non-additive part of the signal.
Gene-gene interactions enter as a static mask plus a perturbation-dependent bias in the network.
MMD regularisation on both the endpoint and the residual distributions keeps population-level structure.
title: Synergy-Aware Residual Flow Matching for Single-Cell Perturbation Prediction (SynGeneFlow)

relevance: The current argument for continuous flows over discrete diffusion on discrete data. Useful context for your choice between a CTMC on the lattice simplex and continuous simplex flows, and it connects to the flow-map papers already on your path.
summary: A continuous flow language model scaled to 8B parameters by adapting a pretrained autoregressive model: causal attention over the prefix and bidirectional, asynchronous flow within each block. Trained on fewer than 30B tokens.
takeaways: Matches or beats the autoregressive base on instruction following, reasoning and coding, and can be distilled into flow maps for one- or few-step generation.
Flow training acts like multi-token prediction and can even improve the AR capabilities it starts from.
A self-speculative decoding scheme (flow drafts, AR verification in one model) gives about 2.5x AR throughput and beats discrete diffusion at comparable quality.
title: Large Flow Language Models (Lafa)

relevance: A cheap upgrade to try in your hierarchical NB + multinomial VAE baseline: swap the standard normal prior for this one and compare ELBOs and cell-type clustering. David Knowles also works on splicing (LeafCutter), so his group may follow up on isoform-level models.
summary: Revisits the VampPrior, which approximates the optimal VAE prior (the aggregate posterior) with a mixture of encoder outputs at learned pseudo-inputs. It fixes two weaknesses: prior and posterior share one amortised covariance, and the mixture weights are fixed and uniform.
takeaways: Decoupling the prior and posterior covariances removes a conflict between wanting high-entropy priors and low-entropy posteriors, and raises model evidence.
Replacing the uniform mixture with a Dirichlet process gives non-parametric clustering in latent space.
Dropping the new prior into scVI improves integration and clustering across six single-cell atlases. Only the prior changes, so it works with any continuous-latent DLVM.
title: VampPrior Unleashed
